person.name: Lina Reyes
person.traits: Under financial pressure. Keeps trading while she talks. Has stopped expecting help.

harmed.prompt: Lina keeps working while you talk - trimming, stacking, not looking up. "I filled out the forms. Bank, police, the online portal." The paper cutter comes down. "Nothing came back from any of them, so sorry ha, I'll keep working while we talk."
harmed.note: You took money from this one, and she runs a business with no room to spare. Every form she filed after your call went unanswered, which is the ordinary experience and the reason people stop filing them.

resistant.prompt: "You're the one about the scam calls?" Lina wipes her hands and comes over to the counter. "Good. I have the number, the times, and what he said, because I was writing up quotes when he called and I just kept writing."
resistant.note: She refused the call you made. She has no loss to report and every reason to help, which makes her easy to work with, but thin as evidence.

unfinished.prompt: Lina glances up from the counter. "A call about a prize, and then nothing. It cut off." She goes back to the stack. "That's three of those this month. They all hang up eventually."
unfinished.note: Your call to her never finished. These calls have become background noise to her, which is what happens when they come often enough.

evidence.label: Three Transfer Receipts
evidence.description: Three outgoing transfers over nine days - a release fee, then a tax charge, then a courier bond - each one described as the last payment required.
evidence.tactic: Advance fee, repeated: every payment buys only the right to be asked for the next one.

evidence.label: Lina's Quote Sheet
evidence.description: The margin of a customer quote: the caller's number, the time, and his phrases in order, written while she kept working.
evidence.tactic: A script written down while it is being read is the one record that can be matched, word for word, to the next call.

evidence.label: Callback Log
evidence.description: Lina's phone log showing four further calls from different numbers in the two weeks after she paid.
evidence.tactic: Paying marks a number as one that pays. The list is worth more once somebody on it has proved they will pay.

resistant.description: Lina's phone log showing four further calls from different numbers in the two weeks after she hung up.

evidence.label: Recovery Offer Message
evidence.description: A later message offering to recover Lina's lost money for an upfront administration fee.
evidence.tactic: A second scam, sold to the victims of the first - and the one that gets the least sympathy and the fewest reports.

tactic_quiz.setup: Three payments in nine days. Each one described, at the time, as the only thing standing between her and the money: [i]"That clears it. Once this is settled the transfer goes out today."[/i]
tactic_quiz.question: Why does a scam like this ask three times instead of asking once for the whole amount?

milestone.title: Tactic Identified: The Escalating Fee
milestone.detail: Recognized that the fee is split deliberately - each payment is small next to what has already been sunk, so the decision never feels like the large one it is.

options.text: Because each new fee looks small next to what she has already sent.
options.feedback: That is the mechanism, and it is why 'why did she send the third one' is the wrong question. By the third, walking away means writing off the first two. Every payment makes the next one easier to justify and harder to refuse.

options.text: Because asking for everything at once would exceed her bank's limit.
options.feedback: Practical, but not the reason. They split the amount long before any limit matters, into sums a bank would let through without a second look.

options.text: Because it gives them more chances to be caught, which they accept.
options.feedback: It is not a cost they put up with - it is the design. More contact means more commitment, not more risk, because the person paying now has a reason to want it to be real.

options.text: Because she asked to pay in installments.
options.feedback: She did not. The installments were offered, and they were offered because a string of small decisions is much easier to get than one big one.
